orderedSlides.text:
The top of the larynx is located higher in the neck in preterm infants
Module: Airway Anatomy and Physiology (Normal and Abnormal)

Source: Coté Chapter 14, p 298 in, Coté, Lerman, Anderson: A Practice of Anesthesia for Infants and Children 2019.

runs.text: The adult airway is more cylindrical whereas the infant airway is a reverse pyramid shape.  This means that the infant airway narrows beneath the level of the glot
tis and can make it difficult to pass an endo tracheal tube.  The narrowing also means that the airway is more sensitive to swelling.

blocks.text: Rhonchi result from air moving through large airways that are partially blocked by mucus/secretions. So they are the result of congestion rather than bronchospasm. While rhonchi are often the result of excess mucus, they are not exclusively heard on inspiration. While they can be heard on both inspiration and expiration, they are often more prevalent on expiration. Since they are due to secretions, they are “wet” sounds and are not like pleural rub (which can be described as dry, harsh, and grating).

orderedBlocks.text: Rhonchi result from air moving through large airways that are partially blocked by mucus/secretions. So they are the result of congestion rather than bronchospasm. While rhonchi are often the result of excess mucus, they are not exclusively heard on inspiration. While they can be heard on both inspiration and expiration, they are often more prevalent on expiration. Since they are due to secretions, they are “wet” sounds and are not like pleural rub (which can be described as dry, harsh, and grating).

orderedContent.text: Upper airway obstruction from residual anesthesia
(possibly, in part, due to body habitus)

leads to inadequate ventilation and CO₂ retention, resulting in hypoxia. It is also important to consider post‑obstructive pulmonary edema (a topic for another day), which would cause diffusion limitation due to fluid in the alveoli making oxygen transfer more difficult.

While post-obstructive pulmonary edema is the main reason these patients are monitored in the PICU and should not be missed, this is less likely than hypoventilation. This should come to mind when repositioning and fixing the hypoventilation does not work! Time for that CXR.

orderedContent.text: Upper airway obstruction from residual anesthesia
(possibly, in part, due to body habitus)

leads to inadequate ventilation and CO₂ retention, resulting in hypoxia. It is also important to consider post‑obstructive pulmonary edema (a topic for another day), which would cause diffusion limitation due to fluid in the alveoli making oxygen transfer more difficult.

While post-obstructive pulmonary edema is the main reason these patients are monitored in the PICU and should not be missed, this is less likely than hypoventilation. This should come to mind when repositioning and fixing the hypoventilation does not work! Time for that CXR.

slides.text:
Pulmonary Anatomy

Module: Respiratory System Overview
Source: [https://dribbble.com/shots/4405245-Human-Respiratory-System].

Parenchyma
External Process- Intra Pleural & Thorax

runs.text: The trachea divides into the right and left primary bronchi, theses then divide further separating into the three lobes on the right (superior, middle, and lower) and two lobes on the right (Upper and lower).   The bronchi continue to divide until they become bronchioles which continue to branch and divide until you reach the alveolus

) and not a patient problem (the ETT or trach is no longer in the correct position, secretions needing suctioning). This can be most easily done by inspecting the tube position and the end tidal CO2. Remember that TCOMs do not rise in real time like an EtCO2 does
and should not be used to determine if your artificial airway is functioning!

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Perform hand hygiene before and after touching the patient’s airway.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Elevate the head of bed to 30 degrees unless contraindicated.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Change ventilator circuits routinely every 48 hours.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Assess daily readiness to extubate and attempt spontaneous breathing trials

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Perform oral care with saline/moistened swabs every 4–8 hours for intubated children.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Monitor cuff pressures regularly for cuffed endotracheal tubes (maintain within recommended range).

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use prophylactic systemic antibiotics to prevent VAP in ventilated patients.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Minimize sedation and perform daily sedation interruption when clinically appropriate.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use closed suction systems for all patients to prevent VAP.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Obtain endotracheal/tracheal aspirate culture before starting antibiotics for suspected VAP, if safe.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Routinely change heat–moisture exchanger (HME) filters daily.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Routinely disconnect the ventilator circuit to reposition the patient.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use enteral feeding protocols and prefer gastric feeding over parenteral nutrition when feasible.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Apply contact precautions for patients colonized or infected with multidrug-resistant organisms.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use prophylactic inhaled antibiotics in intubated patients to prevent VAP.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Perform oral suctioning of pooled secretions prior to repositioning or suctioning ETT.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use a routine schedule of ventilator circuit humidifier changes (e.g., every 24 hours) regardless of condition.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use spontaneous awakening and breathing trial coordination (paired SBT/SAT) as part of daily practice when feasible.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Provide staff education and bundle checklists with regular audit and feedback on VAP prevention practices.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: Use prone positioning routinely to prevent VAP.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
3. Valley of Pulmonara/NURSE VAP Prevention Quiz content.docx
answerProvenance.text: spectrum antibiotics immediately for any new ventilator-associated change without obtaining cultures.

orderedSlides.text:
Definition
Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is defined as a new pneumonia occurring in a patient who has been mechanically ventilated for more than 48 hours.
It is one of the most common hospital-acquired infections in the pediatric population and poses a substantial risk for patients in the PICU.
VAP is particularly concerning due to its association with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and elevated healthcare costs.
It is the second most frequent hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) .

paragraphs: VAP occurs in approximately 5-14% of pediatric patients who are mechanically ventilated for over 48 hours . It affects up to 1 in 10 patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
The incidence of VAP can be higher in children compared to adults, given their unique physiology and potential comorbidities.

The pathogens responsible for VAP can vary, but often include bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and various enteric gram-negative bacteria. Understanding these pathogens is crucial for appropriate treatment and prevention.

orderedSlides.text:
A few statistics to consider:
VAP occurs in approximately 5-14% of pediatric patients who are mechanically ventilated for over 48 hours . It affects up to 1 in 10 patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
The incidence of VAP can be higher in children compared to adults, given their unique physiology and potential comorbidities.
The pathogens responsible for VAP can vary, but often include bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and various enteric gram-negative bacteria. Understanding these pathogens is crucial for appropriate treatment and prevention.

How does VAP develop?
It is primarily due to the aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions containing bacteria. This occurs for several reasons:
Intubation bypasses the body’s normal respiratory defense mechanisms, making it easier for bacteria to colonize the lower respiratory tract.
In addition, factors like impaired consciousness, inadequate oral care, and prolonged ventilation contribute significantly to the risk of VAP.

Other diagnostic considerations
Curr Infect Dis Rep (2015) 17: 41 
In children and neonates, a pediatric VAE (PedVAE) is defined as an increase in the daily minimum mean airway pressure of ≥4 cm H2O sustained for ≥2 calendar days after ≥2 days of stable or decreasing daily minimum mean airway pressure, or an increase in FiO2 of ≥25 points sustained for ≥2 days after ≥2 days of stable or decreasing daily minimum FiO2s.

Hand hygiene 
Upright Positioning: Keeping patients at a 30-45 degree angle helps reduce aspiration risks.
Standardized Oral care: Frequent oral hygiene with chlorhexidine can decrease bacterial colonization in the mouth.

Cuffed ETT 
Daily assessment for extubation
Minimization strategies for sedation and analgesia
Stress Ulcer prophylaxis
Antimicrobial stewardship
Optimize nutrition

Prevention Strategies
Most important strategy is the Implementation of pediatric VAP BUNDLE protocols and interventions that include:
Hand hygiene 
Upright Positioning: Keeping patients at a 30-45 degree angle helps reduce aspiration risks.
Standardized Oral care: Frequent oral hygiene with chlorhexidine can decrease bacterial colonization in the mouth.
Proper airway and circuit management: avoid routine circuit changes
Cuffed ETT 
Daily assessment for extubation
Minimization strategies for sedation and analgesia
Stress Ulcer prophylaxis
Antimicrobial stewardship
Optimize nutrition


By implementing these strategies, we can significantly reduce the incidence of VAP in the PICU.

Now, let’s discuss the potential sequelae of VAP. Patients can experience:

Prolonged Ventilation: Increased duration of mechanical ventilation contributes to further complications.
Increased Length of Stay: VAP can lead to a longer hospital stay, which strains healthcare resources.
Higher Mortality Rates: In severe cases, VAP can be fatal, especially in immunocompromised patients or those with underlying conditions.
Long-term Pulmonary Issues: Some studies suggest that survivors may experience residual pulmonary dysfunction, impacting long-term quality of life.
Increased Health Care Costs: Managing VAP can result in significant financial burdens on families and healthcare systems.

Understanding these sequelae underscores the importance of prevention and early detection. As PICU nurses, you play a vital role in implementing preventive measures and monitoring at-risk patients

orderedSlides.text:
Conclusion
In summary, Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is a serious complication that requires vigilant monitoring and proactive prevention strategies in the PICU. As clinical caregivers, your awareness and actions can make a significant difference in patient outcomes.

slides.text:
Definition
Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is defined as a new pneumonia occurring in a patient who has been mechanically ventilated for more than 48 hours.
It is one of the most common hospital-acquired infections in the pediatric population and poses a substantial risk for patients in the PICU.
VAP is particularly concerning due to its association with increased mortality, prolonged hospital stays, and elevated healthcare costs.
It is the second most frequent hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) .

paragraphs: VAP occurs in approximately 5-14% of pediatric patients who are mechanically ventilated for over 48 hours . It affects up to 1 in 10 patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
The incidence of VAP can be higher in children compared to adults, given their unique physiology and potential comorbidities.

The pathogens responsible for VAP can vary, but often include bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and various enteric gram-negative bacteria. Understanding these pathogens is crucial for appropriate treatment and prevention.

VAP occurs in approximately 5-14% of pediatric patients who are mechanically ventilated for over 48 hours . It affects up to 1 in 10 patients on invasive mechanical ventilation.
The incidence of VAP can be higher in children compared to adults, given their unique physiology and potential comorbidities.
The pathogens responsible for VAP can vary, but often include bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and various enteric gram-negative bacteria. Understanding these pathogens is crucial for appropriate treatment and prevention.

slides.text:
How does VAP develop?
It is primarily due to the aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions containing bacteria. This occurs for several reasons:
Intubation bypasses the body’s normal respiratory defense mechanisms, making it easier for bacteria to colonize the lower respiratory tract.
In addition, factors like impaired consciousness, inadequate oral care, and prolonged ventilation contribute significantly to the risk of VAP.

slides.text:
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of VAP can be challenging. 

Keep in mind that not every new infiltrate indicates VAP, especially if the patient has been on mechanical ventilation for a long period

There is a standardized scoring tool suggested by CDC to help formulate the diagnosis. It is called Clinical Pulmonary Infectious Score (CPIS)

orderedBlocks.text:
Most important strategy is the Implementation of pediatric VAP BUNDLE protocols and interventions that include:
Hand hygiene 
Upright Positioning: Keeping patients at a 30-45 degree angle helps reduce aspiration risks.
Standardized Oral care: Frequent oral hygiene with chlorhexidine can decrease bacterial colonization in the mouth.
Proper airway and circuit management: avoid routine circuit changes
Cuffed ETT 
Daily assessment for extubation
Minimization strategies for sedation and analgesia
Stress Ulcer prophylaxis
Antimicrobial stewardship
Optimize nutrition


By implementing these strategies, we can significantly reduce the incidence of VAP in the PICU.

Hand hygiene 
Upright Positioning: Keeping patients at a 30-45 degree angle helps reduce aspiration risks.
Standardized Oral care: Frequent oral hygiene with chlorhexidine can decrease bacterial colonization in the mouth.
Proper airway and circuit management: avoid routine circuit changes
Cuffed ETT 
Daily assessment for extubation
Minimization strategies for sedation and analgesia
Stress Ulcer prophylaxis
Antimicrobial stewardship
Optimize nutrition


By implementing these strategies, we can significantly reduce the incidence of VAP in the PICU.

runs.text: Increased duration of mechanical ventilation contributes to further complications.

runs.text: VAP can lead to a longer hospital stay, which strains healthcare resources.

runs.text: In severe cases, VAP can be fatal, especially in immunocompromised patients or those with underlying conditions.

paragraphs.text: Higher Mortality Rates: In severe cases, VAP can be fatal, especially in immunocompromised patients or those with underlying conditions.

runs.text: Some studies suggest that survivors may experience residual pulmonary dysfunction, impacting long-term quality of life.

slides.text:
Conclusion
In summary, Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia is a serious complication that requires vigilant monitoring and proactive prevention strategies in the PICU. As clinical caregivers, your awareness and actions can make a significant difference in patient outcomes.

runs.text: You have an 18 year old trauma patient who was intubated overnight for concerns for developing ARDS.   The overnight fellow placed the patient in SIMV-PRVC-PS with a tidal volume of 5 ml/kg, peep of 10, rate of 20 FiO2 is currently at 80% and the patient is saturating 85%. The vent is alarming for Peak Pressures that are being read as too high.

runs.text: You have an 18 year old trauma patient who was intubated overnight for concerns for developing ARDS.   The overnight fellow placed the patient in SIMV-PRVC-PS with a tidal volume of 5 ml/kg, peep of 10, rate of 20 FiO2 is currently at 80% and the patient is saturating 85%. The vent is alarming for Peak Pressures that are being read as too high.

orderedSlides.text:
4. Exposure (Penetration)
	Check if the X-ray beam was strong enough to "see through" the body.
	Vertebrae: You should be able to faintly see the spinal column behind the heart shadow.
	Vessels: Lung markings (blood vessels) should be visible reaching toward the outer edges of the lungs.
	Under-exposure: If the film is too white, the heart and diaphragm will be blurry.
	Over-exposure: If the film is too dark, fine lung details (like early pneumonia) may be missed.

Patient ID, date and time
Includes all important structures
	Lung Apices: The very top of the lungs must 	be included 
	Costophrenic Angles: Both the left and 	right sharp corners where the diaphragm 	meets the ribs must be visible. 
	Borders: The outer edges of the ribs should 	be visible on both sides.

slides.text:
4. Exposure (Penetration)
	Check if the X-ray beam was strong enough to "see through" the body.
	Vertebrae: You should be able to faintly see the spinal column behind the heart shadow.
	Vessels: Lung markings (blood vessels) should be visible reaching toward the outer edges of the lungs.
	Under-exposure: If the film is too white, the heart and diaphragm will be blurry.
	Over-exposure: If the film is too dark, fine lung details (like early pneumonia) may be missed.

What is the appropriate interpretation of this ABG?

answerProvenance.text: A 6-year-old boy is on mechanical ventilation for pneumonia and ARDS. A routine blood gas is drawn. The pH is 7.55 / pCO2 30 / pO2 60 / HCO3- 20. The child has an SBS of -2 on fentanyl and dexmedetomidine. The ventilator has the following settings: PEEP 10 / FIO2 45% / RR 22 / Vt 11mL/kg / PS 15. The child’s respiratory rate is 22. What changes might you expect from medical team?

answerProvenance.text: The correct answer is A, decrease tidal volume. pARDS requires the use of lung protective ventilation, with acceptable tidal volumes ranging from 6-10 mL/kg ideal body weight. This patient has a respiratory alkalosis, and thus the minute ventilation should be decreased. The best way to do that for this patient is to decrease the tidal volume

answerProvenance.text: A previously healthy, 6-year-old girl is on mechanical ventilation for pneumonia and ARDS. A routine blood gas is drawn. The pH is 7.25 / pCO2 60 / HCO3- 26. The child has an SBS of -2 on fentanyl and dexmedetomidine. The ventilator has the following settings: PEEP 10 / FIO2 45% / RR 28 / Vt 8 mL/kg / PS 15. Oxygen saturation is 90%. The child is in the acute phase of ARDS and lung protective ventilation is a priority. What changes might you expect from the medical team?

answerProvenance.text: Correct answer is E, no changes. A pH above 7.2 denotes acceptable gas exchange, allowing for permissive hypercapnia. A respiratory acidosis is present, but the use of lung protective ventilation allows for a range of 6mL/kg ideal body weight tidal volume up to 10mL/kg ideal body weight. This respiratory acidosis does not require action unless the patient has a particular contraindication to allowing hypercarbia. These might include intracranial hypertension or pulmonary hypertension

This respiratory acidosis does not require action unless the patient has a particular contraindication to allowing hypercarbia. These might include intracranial hypertension or pulmonary hypertension

orderedContent.text: This tube is borderline between too deep and just right. It lies directly at the carina. Because this film appears to be of a neonate, retracting the ETT even just a little bit could result in a large change on CXR (or clinically!). Consider discussing a very minor retraction (for example, half a centimeter), or just monitoring the patient.

blocks.text: (1) is pneumonia – this CXR demonstrates a unilateral consolidation. It can be differentiated from atelectasis (2), which may also present with fever, because there is no tracheal deviation towards the consolidation (when there is “socked in” lung, it often pulls surrounding structures down in its collapse as well!). Additionally, atelectasis is often “wedge shaped” because of the collapse of an anatomic area, whereas an infectious pneumonia may not follow these anatomic landmarks.

orderedContent.text: (3) demonstrates a right sided pleural effusion. You can tell it is an effusion because there is loss of the costophrenic angle and

(curved upper border of fluid). If the CXR is shot while flat, you may see “layering” of the fluid in posterior lung fields. If the effusion is large, it may act in the opposite way of atelectasis. Instead of “socking in” and pulling the trachea/mediastinum towards the consolidation, you can think of a large effusion as taking up space and pushing those structures outwards. Thus, you may see deviation of the trachea/mediastinum toward the opposite lung field.

orderedContent.text: (5) demonstrates a pneumothorax. Regardless of why you got a film, spontaneous pneumothorax is a MAJOR finding to look out for! Thus, it is important to remain systematic in every single CXR interpretation. Every time you look at lung fields, remember to trace your lung markings out to the periphery. Here, on the right side, you will notice there is absence of lung markings to the periphery, suggesting a large pneumothorax. This warrants an immediate phone call to a provider.

5. Mount Pneumonora/GAMER-ICU – Mount Pneumonora – Escalating Care.docx
answerProvenance.text: You are caring for Tony, a 4-year-old boy who had a severe submersion injury. He had aspiration of water, received 2 minutes of CPR by a lifeguard with return of circulation and respiratory effort prior to arrival of emergency medical services. He is now intubated, on mechanical ventilation, and under your care in the ICU. He is on synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation, with respiratory rate 18, tidal volume 6 mL/kg, FIO2 50%, and PEEP of 8.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 5. Mount Pneumonora/GAMER-ICU – Mount Pneumonora – Escalating Care.docx
answerProvenance.text: You are alerted by the patient’s telemetry alarms to progressive desaturation He has bilateral lung infiltrates on chest radiograph obtained 40 minutes ago. On your exam, he has coarse inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields, he has bilateral chest rise. He is sedated, but has become increasingly tachycardic. His current vital signs are: HR 125, SPO2 89% on 50% FIO2, ETCO2 60 mmHg, RR 35.

answerProvenance.relativePath: 5. Mount Pneumonora/GAMER-ICU – Mount Pneumonora – Escalating Care.docx
answerProvenance.text: What other information would you like to obtain? Any therapeutic maneuvers?

orderedContent.text: The goal of HFOV is to maintain lung recruitment while minimizing ventilator-induced lung injury.
In conditions like ARDS, alveoli are unstable — they collapse and reopen repeatedly, which causes injury.
HFOV helps prevent that by keeping the lungs open and stable.

orderedContent.text: The goal of HFOV is to maintain lung recruitment while minimizing ventilator-induced lung injury.
In conditions like ARDS, alveoli are unstable — they collapse and reopen repeatedly, which causes injury.
HFOV helps prevent that by keeping the lungs open and stable.

runs.text: You are the code nurse today and respond to a rapid response on the heme/onc floor. You are bringing down a 16 year old male with refractory cancer who is now day 13 s/p bone marrow transplantation (BMT). Per his floor nurse, he has become progressively sleepy, with skin sloughing and diarrhea. The oncologist is concerned for engraftment syndrome. He is now tachypneic, retracting, and hypoxic to 89% on 4L NC. He comes down to PICU with you.

HCO₃⁻ (metabolic)
↓ HCO₃⁻ → acidosis
↑ HCO₃⁻ → alkalosis

orderedBlocks.text:
Step 3:  Is there compensation?

For respiratory acidosis, use this general rule of thumb:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~1 for every +10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~3–4 for every +10
Respiratory alkalosis:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~2 for every −10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~4–5

If compensation doesn’t match → mixed disorder

orderedBlocks.text:
This patient’s OI is 14.
Recall that:
 OI = [Fio2 (whole number, not as a percent) x Mean Airway Pressure] / PaO2
Therefore, OI = (50x14)/48 = 14

Pediatric ARDS can be classified using OI. Our patient has moderate ARDS. 
OI 4-8 = mild ARDS
OI 8-16 = moderate ARDS
OI >16 = severe ARDS

minimize barotrauma or volutrauma to the lungs with poor compliance, limit free radical toxicity from too much FiO2, while ensuring adequate oxygenation.

ARDS guidelines:
pH: we often accept mild acidosis (>~7.2) if the patient is hemodynamically stable and not requiring vasoactive support. If the heart is unhappy, we worry more about correcting the acidosis to ensure sufficient cardiac output. 

pCO2: Some people refer to the “rule of 60s” in ARDS. 
We accept PcO2 <60 and a PaO2> 60. Thus, mild hypercarbia is permitted if the lungs are non-compliant, as evidenced here by a physiologic Vt (7 ml/kg) and relatively high peak pressures (27). Do no damage!

PaO2: Goal >60 if able! Recall that free radical toxicity has been shown for prolonged fio2> 60%, so here the best way to improve oxygenation ⟶ increase MAP ⟶ PEEP is the biggest component of MAP!

orderedSlides.text:
ARDS guidelines:
pH: we often accept mild acidosis (>~7.2) if the patient is hemodynamically stable and not requiring vasoactive support. If the heart is unhappy, we worry more about correcting the acidosis to ensure sufficient cardiac output. 

pCO2: Some people refer to the “rule of 60s” in ARDS. 
We accept PcO2 <60 and a PaO2> 60. Thus, mild hypercarbia is permitted if the lungs are non-compliant, as evidenced here by a physiologic Vt (7 ml/kg) and relatively high peak pressures (27). Do no damage!

PaO2: Goal >60 if able! Recall that free radical toxicity has been shown for prolonged fio2> 60%, so here the best way to improve oxygenation ⟶ increase MAP ⟶ PEEP is the biggest component of MAP!

NEXT
Answer continued

runs.text: You are the code nurse today and respond to a rapid response on the heme/onc floor. You are bringing down a 16 year old male with refractory cancer who is now day 13 s/p bone marrow transplantation (BMT). Per his floor nurse, he has become progressively sleepy, with skin sloughing and diarrhea. The oncologist is concerned for engraftment syndrome. He is now tachypneic, retracting, and hypoxic to 89% on 4L NC. He comes down to PICU with you.

orderedBlocks.text:
Step 3:  Is there compensation?

For respiratory acidosis, use this general rule of thumb:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~1 for every +10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~3–4 for every +10
Respiratory alkalosis:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~2 for every −10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~4–5

If compensation doesn’t match → mixed disorder

Step 3:  Is there compensation?

For respiratory acidosis, use this general rule of thumb:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~1 for every +10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by ~3–4 for every +10
Respiratory alkalosis:
If acute: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~2 for every −10 pCO₂
If chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↓ by ~4–5

If compensation doesn’t match → mixed disorder

orderedBlocks.text:
This patient’s OI is 14.
Recall that:
 OI = [Fio2 (whole number, not as a percent) x Mean Airway Pressure] / PaO2
Therefore, OI = (50x14)/48 = 14

Pediatric ARDS can be classified using OI. Our patient has moderate ARDS. 
OI 4-8 = mild ARDS
OI 8-16 = moderate ARDS
OI >16 = severe ARDS

This blood gas represents a primary respiratory acidosis. Given this patient has moderate ARDS, we begin to think about our “do no harm” strategies:
minimize barotrauma or volutrauma to the lungs with poor compliance, limit free radical toxicity from too much FiO2, while ensuring adequate oxygenation.

ARDS guidelines:
pH: we often accept mild acidosis (>~7.2) if the patient is hemodynamically stable and not requiring vasoactive support. If the heart is unhappy, we worry more about correcting the acidosis to ensure sufficient cardiac output. 

pCO2: Some people refer to the “rule of 60s” in ARDS. 
We accept PcO2 <60 and a PaO2> 60. Thus, mild hypercarbia is permitted if the lungs are non-compliant, as evidenced here by a physiologic Vt (7 ml/kg) and relatively high peak pressures (27). Do no damage!

PaO2: Goal >60 if able! Recall that free radical toxicity has been shown for prolonged fio2> 60%, so here the best way to improve oxygenation ⟶ increase MAP ⟶ PEEP is the biggest component of MAP!

slides.text:
ARDS guidelines:
pH: we often accept mild acidosis (>~7.2) if the patient is hemodynamically stable and not requiring vasoactive support. If the heart is unhappy, we worry more about correcting the acidosis to ensure sufficient cardiac output. 

pCO2: Some people refer to the “rule of 60s” in ARDS. 
We accept PcO2 <60 and a PaO2> 60. Thus, mild hypercarbia is permitted if the lungs are non-compliant, as evidenced here by a physiologic Vt (7 ml/kg) and relatively high peak pressures (27). Do no damage!

PaO2: Goal >60 if able! Recall that free radical toxicity has been shown for prolonged fio2> 60%, so here the best way to improve oxygenation ⟶ increase MAP ⟶ PEEP is the biggest component of MAP!

NEXT
Answer continued

You are preparing to monitor Mateo during the ERT. Which set of monitored alarms/events are most critical to
during the trial, and which parameters define a passing ERT?
At baseline (start): RR 30, SpO2 96%, measured tidal volume (Vt) ≈ 5 ml/kg, EtCO2 42 mmHg.
At 10 minutes: RR increases to 40, SpO2 transiently dips to 94% for 15 seconds with prompt stimulation and suctioning; no bradycardia; EtCO2 rises to 46 mmHg.
At 18 minutes: brief central pause in breathing lasting 6 seconds without desaturation (SpO2 maintained ≥95%) and no alarm or intervention required.
At 25 minutes: Vt measured at 4.2 ml/kg, SpO2 95%, EtCO2 48 mmHg (increase from baseline 6 mmHg).
At 60 minutes: RR 38, SpO2 95%, Vt 4.0–4.5 ml/kg, EtCO2 50 mmHg (overall increase from baseline 8 mmHg). No apneas with desaturation events occurred during the trial.

Over the last 24 hours he has improved and the team has been able to wean his ventilatory support. The day team considered if he might be ready for an extubation readiness trial (ERT) during rounds. orderedContent.text: A. An ERT is a short trial of full ventilator support to confirm stability; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤8, FiO2 ≤60%, SaO2 ≥90%, no spontaneous effort required, and sedation deep.

runs.text: A. An ERT is a short trial of full ventilator support to confirm stability; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤8, FiO2 ≤60%, SaO2 ≥90%, no spontaneous effort required, and sedation deep.

blocks.text: A. An ERT is a short trial of full ventilator support to confirm stability; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤8, FiO2 ≤60%, SaO2 ≥90%, no spontaneous effort required, and sedation deep.

orderedContent.text: B. An ERT is a monitored spontaneous breathing trial to assess if a patient can breathe without full ventilator support; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤6 cm H2O, FiO2 ≤50%, SaO2 ≥95% on current settings, presence of spontaneous respiratory effort, hemodynamically stable, sedation at goal (arousable), and no planned significantly invasive procedures within the next day shift.

runs.text: B. orderedContent.text: C. An ERT is a protocolized increase in pressure support to test cough strength; screen is favorable if PEEP ≤4, FiO2 ≤30%, SaO2 ≥98%, and only if the patient is sedated.
